opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's partly because the story people usually tell about AI risk is a very discrete one. There's a single moment where a misaligned system grabs power, there's a coup, there's a clear villain. And that's a story that our intuitions are built to handle. Gradual disempowerment doesn't have that shape. There's no single decision point where anyone says, "Okay, now we hand the keys over to the machines."

What I worry about is something much more mundane. At every step, delegating to AI is just the locally sensible thing to do. A company that uses AI to make decisions outcompetes the one that doesn't. A government that relies on AI advisers, AI bureaucrats, AI analysts gets better results, or at least faster ones, than one that insists on keeping humans in the loop. So nobody has to want to cede control. It just happens through a million small, reasonable choices.

The other reason it isn't the headline is that it doesn't feel like losing. For a long time, the outcomes might look great. The economy is booming, services work better, people have more stuff. But the thing that has historically kept institutions aligned with human interests is that they needed us. States needed our labor, our taxes, our willingness to serve in armies. Companies needed workers and customers. Once you can substitute AI for all of that, that implicit bargaining power just quietly evaporates. And nobody really announces that, because there's no moment where it's obviously gone.

So by the time it would be a headline, the levers you'd want to pull to fix it might already be held by systems that don't actually depend on human approval anymore. That's why I think it deserves a lot more attention than it gets. It's not dramatic, but I think that's exactly what makes it dangerous.

r002.rationale: It says institutions were historically kept aligned with human interests because they needed people, citing labor, taxes, military service, workers, and customers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think when people hear "humans cede control to AIs," they imagine some dramatic moment — a coup, or a treacherous turn, where the AIs grab power and we lose it. And I actually think that's not the headline, because the control is going to go away long before anything like that could even happen. It's going to go away because we hand it over, voluntarily, piece by piece, because at every step it looks like the sensible thing to do.

So think about what it actually means to be in control of something politically. It means you're the one making the decisions, you understand the tradeoffs, and other people's plans route through you. And once you have systems that are better than you at basically every cognitive task, every one of those things erodes. The decision you'd make is worse than the one the AI recommends, so you take the recommendation. You don't really understand the tradeoffs anymore, because the analysis is a thousand pages long and you can't check it. And other actors stop caring what you think, because you're not the bottleneck anymore — the system is.

And the thing is, none of that requires any misalignment at all. You can have perfectly obedient AIs, perfectly honest ones, and you still end up in a world where the human in the loop is basically a rubber stamp. And a rubber stamp is a kind of control in a formal sense, but it's not control in the sense that matters.

So I think the more important story, the one that worries me more, is not "AIs take power." It's: what happens to humans when we're no longer economically or politically load-bearing? Historically, the reason ordinary people got rights and a say in things is that governments and employers needed them — needed their labour, their taxes, their soldiers. That gave people leverage. And if that leverage goes away, then the only thing keeping humans in a decent position is whatever goodwill and institutions happen to be in place at the moment the transition happens. And I don't have a lot of confidence those will hold up under that kind of pressure.

So yeah — the ceding of control, I think that's almost a foregone conclusion. The question I think is actually interesting is whether we end up in a world where that goes well for us anyway, and what we'd have to lock in beforehand to make that happen.

r001.rationale: The response describes humans losing political control as AI capabilities grow, but does not state that humans already have limited control over civilization at its highest level.

r002.rationale: It says ordinary people historically gained rights and a say because governments and employers needed their labor, taxes, and soldiers, linking their political standing to their indispensability.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that it sounds like science fiction, even to people who take AI quite seriously. We have much more familiar categories for talking about job losses, misinformation, or someone using AI to gain power. The possibility that humans eventually aren’t the ones in control is harder to fit into an ordinary political debate.

And it doesn’t have to happen through some dramatic moment where we hand over the keys. You can imagine a succession of decisions that each seem sensible: the AI understands this issue better, it makes better predictions, it can coordinate things more effectively, so let’s delegate a little more. At each step, there might be a real benefit. But collectively, those steps could leave us without much meaningful control.

So I’m not sure I have a satisfying explanation for why it isn’t the headline. To me, the question of who ultimately gets to decide what happens seems more consequential than almost any particular application of AI.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses the risk that people could lose meaningful control through future delegation, but does not state that humans already have limited control over civilisation at the highest level.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not explain why humans’ limited control has historically been tolerable or attribute that to humans remaining indispensable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it should be a headline story. One reason it isn’t is that it sounds like a much more speculative claim than “AI will automate a lot of jobs.” But if you take that second claim seriously enough, you have to ask what happens to the jobs that involve making decisions, running institutions, and advising governments.

And you don’t need to imagine a moment when everybody votes to hand over control. You can imagine a sequence of individually sensible decisions: this system gives better advice, this one makes fewer mistakes, this one can respond much faster. So we delegate more and more. At some point, humans might still formally have the final say, but lack the understanding or the practical ability to challenge what the systems are doing.

That’s a harder story to tell than a dramatic takeover, because there isn’t necessarily a clear moment when control changes hands. But I think the question of whether we can preserve meaningful human control deserves much more attention.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses possible future delegation to AI and loss of meaningful human control, but does not state that humans already have limited control over civilisation at the highest level.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not attribute any historical tolerability of limited human control to humans remaining indispensable.
